items.question: What topics are to be treated in the twentieth chapter?
premises: The twentieth chapter deals with preparation ending in the examination of eligibility.
It also treats the rite of the balance.
These form the whole subject matter to be spoken there.
items.inference: The twentieth chapter will present the preparation culminating in eligibility-examination and the rite of the balance.
uncertainties: The exact ritual sense of tulāvidhiḥ may be more specific than 'rite of the balance'.
items.plain_english: In the twentieth chapter, the full subject matter will be the preparation that culminates in examining eligibility, together with the rite of the balance.

items.question: What procedures are set forth in the twenty-first chapter?
premises: The twenty-first chapter includes the rite concerning the dead and the living and the net.
It includes instruction in the levels and a group of consecratory rites.
It also includes an investigation of strength and weakness.
items.inference: The twenty-first chapter sets forth these rites and investigations as its procedure.
uncertainties: The technical meaning of jāla and padeśa is compressed in this summary verse.
items.plain_english: In the twenty-first chapter, the procedure will cover the rite of the dead and the living, the net, instruction in the levels, the group of consecrations, and the investigation of strength and weakness.

items.question: Which matters are to be clearly explained in the procedure of removing the liṅga?
premises: The procedure of removing the liṅga includes hearing and authorization.
It includes purification and removal of sin.
It also includes the cutting away of doubt.
items.inference: These matters are to be clearly explained in the liṅga-removal procedure.
uncertainties: liṅga here may refer to a ritual emblem or to a subtler mark, depending on context.
items.plain_english: In the procedure for removing the liṅga, the text will clearly explain hearing, authorization, purification, removal of sin, and the cutting away of doubt.

items.question: What subjects are covered in the rite of consecration for the sādhaka?
premises: The rite includes examination and appointment of the teacher.
It includes the teacher's vow and the removal of a mistaken view.
It includes classification and the state of being a sādhaka.
items.inference: The sādhaka-consecration rite covers these matters of teacher, vow, correction, classification, and sādhaka status.
uncertainties: haraṇaṃ mateḥ could mean removal of a doctrine, opinion, or mental disposition.
items.plain_english: In the rite of consecration for the sādhaka, the topics will include examining and appointing the teacher, the teacher's vow, removing a mistaken view, its classification, and the state of being a sādhaka.

items.question: What is to be treated in the twenty-fourth chapter called the final rite?
premises: The twenty-fourth chapter is named the final rite.
It concerns the qualified person.
It concerns consecration and its purpose.
items.inference: The twenty-fourth chapter will treat the qualified person, consecration, and the purpose of that consecration.
uncertainties: antyayāga may refer to a final worship, funeral rite, or concluding ritual, depending on tradition.
items.plain_english: In the twenty-fourth chapter, called the final rite, the text will discuss the qualified person, consecration, and the purpose of that consecration.

items.question: What is the subject matter of the twenty-fifth chapter on śrāddha?
premises: The twenty-fifth chapter expounds śrāddha.
Its purpose is the giving of enjoyment and liberation.
Its procedure is presented clearly.
items.inference: The twenty-fifth chapter gives a clear summary of śrāddha, its purpose, and its procedure.
uncertainties: bhogamokṣadāna may refer to benefits for the deceased, the performer, or both.
items.plain_english: In the twenty-fifth chapter, which expounds śrāddha, the text will clearly present its purpose as giving enjoyment and liberation, along with its procedure.

items.question: What topics are included in the discussion of daily worship and its supports?
premises: The discussion includes the purpose of daily worship for one who still has remaining duties.
It includes supreme worship on the ritual ground and the nature of the liṅga.
It also includes a many-sided explanation of the rosary.
items.inference: The section treats daily worship together with its purpose, setting, liṅga, and rosary.
uncertainties: śeṣavṛtteḥ is terse and may refer to a householder or one with continuing obligations.
items.plain_english: This section will explain the purpose of daily worship for one who still has duties, supreme worship on the ritual ground, the nature of the liṅga in many ways, and the meaning of the rosary.

items.question: What is to be explained in the exposition of liṅga worship and occasional rites?
premises: The exposition of liṅga worship includes divisions of worship.
It then turns to occasional rites.
Those occasional rites are treated by classification, purpose, and procedure.
items.inference: The exposition covers both liṅga worship and the classification, purpose, and procedure of occasional rites.
uncertainties: The boundary between liṅgārcā and naimittika rites is only implied here.
items.plain_english: In the exposition of liṅga worship, the text will explain the divisions of worship, and then the classification, purpose, and procedure of occasional rites.

items.question: Which festival and worship topics are explained in this section?
premises: The section treats divisions of festivals and their specific forms.
It treats wheel worship and its worship procedure.
It explains the purpose of worship on guru days and other beginning and end days.
items.inference: This section explains festival divisions, wheel worship, and the purpose of special-day worship.
uncertainties: cakracarcā may refer to a specific tantric circle rite rather than a general wheel worship.
items.plain_english: This section will explain the divisions of festivals and their details, wheel worship and its performance, and the purpose of worship on guru days and other special beginning and end days.

items.question: What rites and procedures are included in this part of the occasional teachings?
premises: The section includes examination of death.
It includes the rite of the gathering of yoginīs and related practices.
It includes procedures for exposition, hearing, and guru worship.
items.inference: This part gathers rites concerning death, yoginī gatherings, teaching, hearing, and guru worship.
uncertainties: yogīśīmelaka is a technical ritual term whose exact form may vary by tradition.
items.plain_english: This part will cover the examination of death, the rite of the yoginī gathering and related practices, and the procedures for exposition, hearing, and guru worship.

items.question: What is established in the twenty-eighth chapter on occasional rites?
premises: The twenty-eighth chapter is called the exposition of occasional rites.
It treats distinctions concerning the qualified self.
It also treats the order of the lineage of the siddha's consort.
items.inference: The twenty-eighth chapter establishes teachings on the qualified self and the siddha-consort lineage.
uncertainties: siddhapatnīkulakramaḥ may denote a ritual lineage, a goddess lineage, or both.
items.plain_english: In the twenty-eighth chapter, called the exposition of occasional rites, the text sets out distinctions concerning the qualified self and the order of the lineage of the siddha's consort.

items.question: What teachings are presented in the twenty-ninth chapter?
premises: The twenty-ninth chapter includes procedures of worship and messenger rites.
It includes the order of the secret upaniṣad.
It includes initiation, consecration, and awakening.
items.inference: The twenty-ninth chapter presents ritual procedures together with secret teaching and awakening.
uncertainties: dautavidhi may refer to rites involving a messenger or emissary; the exact ritual is unclear.
items.plain_english: In the twenty-ninth chapter, the text will present the procedures of worship and messenger rites, the order of the secret upaniṣad, initiation, consecration, and awakening.

items.question: What is explained in the thirtieth chapter?
premises: The thirtieth chapter explains the nature of mantra.
It explains the power of mantra.
It also explains divisions such as trident and lotus, and figures such as sky-hare and svastika.
items.inference: The thirtieth chapter explains mantra's nature and power along with related symbolic divisions.
uncertainties: vyomaśaśa is an obscure technical term; 'sky-hare' is a tentative gloss.
items.plain_english: In the thirtieth chapter, the text explains the nature of mantra and its power, along with divisions such as the trident and lotus and figures such as the sky-hare and svastika.

items.question: What is to be stated at length in the thirty-first chapter?
premises: The thirty-first chapter treats distinctions of subordinate and principal status.
It treats essential nature.
It treats power and worship.
items.inference: The thirty-first chapter will give an extended account of status-distinctions, nature, power, and worship.
uncertainties: The exact referent of guṇapradhānatābhedāḥ depends on the preceding technical context.
items.plain_english: In the thirty-first chapter, the text will explain at length the distinctions of subordinate and principal status, essential nature, and power and worship.

items.question: Why is no further division stated in the exposition of the mudrās?
premises: The exposition of the mudrās declares divisions of the kalās.
Its scope runs from the thirty-two principles up to Īśa.
Within that scope the matter is already very clear.
items.inference: Because the exposition from the thirty-two principles to Īśa is already clear, no further division is stated there.
uncertainties: The exact parsing of dvātriṃśatattvādīśākhyātprabhṛti is compressed and may reflect a technical doctrinal range.
items.plain_english: In the exposition of the mudrās, the divisions of the kalās are declared; and because the treatment from the thirty-two principles up to Īśa is already very clear, no further division is added.

items.question: Why is no other outline stated at this point in the text?
premises: There is no further division to be made there.
The subject matter is primary and must be known.
The sequence of other eligibilities follows from that.
items.inference: No other outline is stated here because the primary matter is clear and the sequence of further eligibilities is already implied.
uncertainties: adhikārāntarakramaḥ could refer to a sequence of topics or of qualified practitioners.
items.plain_english: Since there is no further division there, no other outline is stated here; that matter is primary and must be known, and from it follows the sequence of other eligibilities.

items.question: What follows after the outline of topics has been declared?
premises: The outline procedure has been declared for easy comprehension.
The next task concerns the defining marks of the subject.
Those defining marks are to be explained in due order.
items.inference: After the outline, the text proceeds to explain the defining marks in order.
items.plain_english: Thus the outline has been given for easy understanding; now the defining marks of this subject will be explained in due order.

items.question: How are the self, bondage, and liberation defined in this summary teaching?
premises: The self abides as the partless light of awareness and possesses a host of powers as its own nature.
By concealing its own greatness, that same self appears in a bound form.
By revealing its luminous nature, it attains liberation, which appears manifold in a manifold field.
items.inference: The self is intrinsically free awareness; bondage is self-concealment, and liberation is self-revelation expressed in manifold ways.
uncertainties: citrākārasya citraḥ is compressed and may refer to varied means, experiences, or manifestations of liberation.
items.plain_english: The self is the partless light of awareness, whose own nature is a host of powers. By hiding its own greatness it appears bound, and by revealing its luminous nature it is liberated. This liberation shows itself in many forms within a manifold world; that, in brief, is the teaching presented here.

items.question: How does false knowledge create the appearance of impurity, and how is that appearance removed?
premises: False knowledge is like a cataract that produces defects in vision.
Because of that defect, even what is pure appears as a seat of impurity.
If the cataract-like defect in vision is removed, the object is seen rightly.
items.inference: Impurity is an appearance caused by defective vision; when that defect is removed, no suspicion of impurity remains.
uncertainties: The verse uses medical and epistemic imagery together; the mapping is analogical rather than literal.
items.plain_english: False knowledge is like a cataract: it creates defects in vision, so that even what is pure seems impure. But if that cataract-like defect in seeing is removed, how could any suspicion of impurity remain?

items.question: Why is it mistaken to call the multitude of beings insentient?
premises: The multitude of beings forcibly seizes hearts, makes them dance, and conceals the heart of the self in playful gestures.
Such activity shows liveliness rather than insentience.
Calling it insentient reflects the speaker's own dullness, though even that dullness could ironically suggest likeness to the divine play.
items.inference: The world of beings is not insentient; to call it so is a mistake born of the speaker's own insensitivity.
uncertainties: bhāvavrāta is addressed poetically; it may mean the totality of phenomena or beings.
The final irony about jaḍātmatā as praise is rhetorically compressed.
items.plain_english: O multitude of beings, you seize people's hearts, make them dance with many gestures, conceal the heart of the self, and play. Anyone who calls you insentient is himself insentient and poorly taught. I would even say that if he has any insentient nature, it could only count as praise insofar as it suggests some likeness to you.

items.question: Who is authorized to undertake this investigation, and why is that restriction necessary?
premises: Only teachers whose impurity has fallen away and who know higher and lower realities are authorized.
Such teachers are grounded in the true being of Śiva.
Without such qualification, investigation becomes fruitless and leads to hatred, blame, loss, and supplication.
items.inference: This investigation is restricted to purified, Śiva-grounded teachers because unqualified inquiry produces harmful and fruitless results.
uncertainties: The final compound dveṣakalaṃkahāniyācñā is compact; the exact nuance of yācñā here may be supplication or pleading.
items.plain_english: In this teaching, only teachers whose impurities have fallen away, who know the higher and the lower, and who are grounded in the true being of Śiva are authorized to investigate. Without that qualification, the inquiry is fruitless and leads to hatred, blame, loss, and begging.
